newsitem.title: FRANCE: French assembly accepts disputed immigration bill.
newsitem.headline: French assembly accepts disputed immigration bill.

text.p: The French National Assembly on Thursday approved a hotly disputed immigration reform bill by a vote of 113 to 61, sending the bill on to the Senate for more debate and a final reading beginning on March 11.

The bill passed on the third day of often acrimonious debate, over the opposition of French leftist deputies, who urged the centre-right government to withdraw it after artists and intellectuals launched petition drives and took to the streets to denounce the measure in a series of protest marches.

A protest on Saturday drew around 100,000 peaceful demonstrators but a second march on Tuesday night turned violent when riot police clashed with marchers throwing rocks at them, injuring 30 police officers.

Groups opposed to the measure, which aims to close loopholes in tough existing laws dating from 1993 and would grant the police extended powers to track immigrants in France, have scheduled another mass protest for Sunday in the French capital.
The measure has triggered a broad, emotional debate in France on racism and xenophobia at a time of a near-record jobless rate of 12.7 percent, soaring social welfare costs and rising violent crime.

France's conservative government defends it as needed to close loopholes in the current law. It also has at various times portrayed it as a lent crime.jobs bill and as a way to discourage citizens of third world countries who might be considering sneaking into France to take advantage of its generous welfare benefits.
But opponents accuse the government of pandering to the growing numbers of voters for the extreme-right National Front with an eye on general elections in 1998.
They say the measure would encourage citizens to develop racial hatreds and to fear foreigners.
Socialist leader Lionel Jospin pledged to do away with the bill if his party wins a general election due in March next year.
The Association of University Presidents jumped into the fray by approving a motion at its annual conference urging France to retain policies favouring open international educational exchanges.
Debate had been slow in the National Assembly, with opposition leftists seeking to delay the bill or scupper it with amendments.
Most amendments were thrown out but one was approved allowing illegal immigrants who have been in France for more than 15 years to obtain residence permits.
The provision had been in the bill as drafted by the government but was knocked out by Senate hardliners during its first reading.
Also approved was a key article authorising police to keep the passports or travel documents of illegal immigrants and allowing searches of commercial vehicles within 20 km (12 miles) of the border.
The article also authorises police to take the fingerprints of foreigners from outside the European Union who apply for a residence permit.

Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said he would ask other European Union foreign ministers to consider reining in the European Parliament after it approved a motion urging France to drop the immigration bill.
He said he wanted his fellow ministers "to reflect on the European Parliament's exceeding its responsibilities".
